web-service.title: Scaling a Modern Web Application
web-service.subtitle: System Design Interview: From Simple Monolith to Distributed Async Architecture
web-service.problemStatement: Design a scalable web platform where clients perform queries and updates with low latency, then introduce caching for hot reads and asynchronous workers for background tasks.

steps.name: Single-Server MVP
steps.interviewerPrompt: Let's start with the basics: Design a service where clients can query data and perform updates with low latency.
steps.solution: Establish the synchronous request path: Client sends HTTP requests to a stateless CPU API server, which reads and writes directly to the primary database.
tradeoffs: Single point of failure (SPOF) at the database layer
Read queries compete with write transactions for locks and disk I/O
Zero caching: repeated identical reads hit disk every time

diagram.name: Scaling a Modern Web Application / Trace a minimal API
diagram.description: Synthetic requests call an API, a TTL cache with asynchronous replica origin, and a leased task queue with an idempotent result store. Cache/replica timing is an authored approximation.

steps.name: Caching & Read Replicas
steps.interviewerPrompt: Our read traffic just surged 10x (90% reads, 10% writes). Database CPU is spiking at 95% and queries are timing out. How do we scale reads?
steps.solution: Introduce an in-memory TTL cache (e.g. Redis) using the Cache-Aside pattern, and split database traffic with asynchronous read replicas.
tradeoffs: Cache invalidation challenges (TTL expiration vs. explicit invalidation)
Replication lag: eventual consistency means clients might read slightly stale data immediately after a write
Cache stampede (dogpiling) when hot keys expire concurrently

steps.name: Separate committed work from a lost reply
steps.stage: Separate committed work from a lost reply
steps.interviewerPrompt: Which result is uncertain, and which state remains authoritative after reply delivery fails?
steps.solution: Drop replies briefly after work may have executed. A timeout establishes an uncertain acknowledgement, not proof that an effect did not occur. Inspect attempts and retained state; retries must preserve their operation identity.
tradeoffs: Asynchronous response model: clients must poll or subscribe via WebSockets for job completion
Idempotency: workers must handle duplicate delivery safely using unique idempotency keys
Backpressure and poison-pill messages: unhandled tasks must route to DLQ after N retries

diagram.name: Scaling a Modern Web Application / Separate committed work from a lost reply
diagram.description: Synthetic requests call an API, a TTL cache with asynchronous replica origin, and a leased task queue with an idempotent result store. Cache/replica timing is an authored approximation.

steps.name: Asynchronous Task Queue & Workers
steps.interviewerPrompt: Users are triggering heavy background tasks (PDF generation, webhook dispatches, data processing) that take 5 to 30 seconds. API connection pools are exhausting. How do we decouple?
steps.solution: Add an asynchronous leased task queue (e.g. SQS/RabbitMQ) with a dedicated pool of background workers writing to an idempotent results store, plus a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for failed retries.
tradeoffs: Asynchronous response model: clients must poll or subscribe via WebSockets for job completion
Idempotency: workers must handle duplicate delivery safely using unique idempotency keys
Backpressure and poison-pill messages: unhandled tasks must route to DLQ after N retries

chat-application.title: Real-Time Streaming Chat System
chat-application.subtitle: System Design Interview: Persistent Conversations, Inference Pool, and Token Streaming
chat-application.problemStatement: Design a real-time messaging platform (like Slack or Discord) supporting 1M concurrent connections, persistent conversation history, and live token streaming.

steps.name: Persist identity and stream a bounded reply
steps.stage: Persist identity and stream a bounded reply
steps.interviewerPrompt: Design the core chat service: User submits prompts, authenticates, and conversation history is reliably saved.
steps.solution: Check conversation membership at the API and storage boundaries, persist the prompt, then deliver acknowledged synthetic chunks before committing the assistant reply. One generator serves this baseline; authorization failures remain visible.
tradeoffs: Storage remains the authority for tenant membership and ordered messages; an earlier API decision cannot bypass a later denied storage check.
A single generator is easy to inspect but serial chunk requests share its capacity. This model generates fixed text and does not execute an LLM.

diagram.name: Real-Time Streaming Chat System / Persist a conversation
diagram.description: Conversation membership, durable messages and stream lifecycle have separate authoritative owners. Bounded model admission, two generation replicas and client delivery execute through real drawn edges. No live accounts or LLM.

notes.text: Access/history and stream lifecycle are separate executable owners. Crash a model replica, stream session, delivery router or conversation store independently. Inspect durable messages and client chunks: a delivered chunk is not an assistant commit. All text remains deterministic synthetic content.

steps.name: Admit and route generation requests
steps.interviewerPrompt: We need to connect LLM workers to generate replies, but different models have different latencies and GPU capacity limits.
steps.solution: Route each chunk request through bounded quota admission and a round-robin replica pool. Both generators use identical chunk framing so routing cannot change the durable reply or cursor contract.
tradeoffs: Extra generation replicas share one conversation authority and stable framing; independent histories would fork durable state.
A request quota models admission, not GPU memory allocation, model checkpoints or speculative inference.

rag-assistant.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) System
rag-assistant.subtitle: System Design Interview: From Baseline Model to Vector Retrieval & Reranking Ingestion
rag-assistant.problemStatement: Design an enterprise AI search assistant that embeds queries, searches vector document candidates, reranks results, and streams validated responses under 200ms.

steps.name: Generate a bounded structured response
steps.interviewerPrompt: Let's build an AI assistant that answers user questions with structured schema validation.
steps.solution: Questions pass through API and worker admission into structured generation and validation. The independent synthetic document source already feeds chunking and index updates, but this baseline query path does not read the index.
tradeoffs: The direct query path avoids retrieval calls but has no modeled document grounding. Inspect generated output validation and request failures separately from knowledge quality.
Background chunking and index publication consume modeled work even though queries do not use them in this stage. No generated answer is evidence of factual correctness.

diagram.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) System / Generate a validated response
diagram.description: Synthetic RAG application with CPU/GPU stages, batched embedding, vector-index queries, reranking and structured model output. A document feed shares the same embedding/index services through a bounded chunker; no actual inference or semantic retrieval occurs.

steps.name: Account for retrieval calls and publication delay
steps.stage: Account for retrieval calls and publication delay
steps.interviewerPrompt: We need the assistant to cite internal documents accurately. How do we retrieve the right context?
steps.solution: Connect a coordinator that calls embedding, index search and generation in order. Search returns candidate counts and index-age metadata; these determine modeled context size and latency. Published and pending vector counts expose the effect of asynchronous ingestion, not actual retrieved passages.
tradeoffs: The additional calls consume service capacity and increase latency before generation. The top-K and chunk-token assumptions determine modeled prompt size.
Publication delay can make a query observe older index counts. This is a bounded freshness model, not a relevance or recall evaluation.

video-distribution.title: Global Video Streaming & CDN Architecture
video-distribution.subtitle: System Design Interview: Regional CDN POPs, Global Distribution, and Peer-Assisted Delivery
video-distribution.problemStatement: Design a global video streaming platform (like YouTube or Netflix) with regional CDN edge caching, origin shielding, and peer-assisted playback offloading.

steps.name: Share one edge cache and origin shield
steps.stage: Share one edge cache and origin shield
steps.interviewerPrompt: Design a video streaming service where viewers stream HLS/DASH video chunks without overwhelming the storage origin.
steps.solution: Both viewer cohorts read manifests and fetch numbered segments through one admitted edge cache. Cache misses share a retry-protected origin shield and an origin admission limit. Inspect cache hits, coalesced fetches and completed playback before splitting regions.
tradeoffs: A cold segment still pays edge, shield and origin transfer time. Coalescing reduces repeated origin requests for concurrent misses under the configured demand.
Both cohorts share one admission and cache boundary, so their offered work competes there. This stage does not measure geographic placement or egress prices.

diagram.name: Global Video Streaming & CDN Architecture / Deliver edge-cached segments
diagram.description: Three thousand viewers are split into two independently faultable regions. Playback requires a real manifest receipt; regional caches fetch through one shield and origin. Peer availability and admission are distinct from CDN delivery. Bytes are aggregate unicast, not measured video transport.

notes.text: Regional peers only assist cohorts in their own pool. Manifest metadata, regional cache copies and the shared shield are distinct state. Viewer CDN KiB plus peer KiB is end-user delivery; do not sum every network hop as unique delivered content. Crash either peer pool, either cache or the manifest independently. No codec, signaling, ICE or DRM is modeled.

steps.name: Give each region an edge cache
steps.stage: Give each region an edge cache
steps.interviewerPrompt: Traffic is scaling globally with spikes in East and West regions. How do we reduce cross-continent latency?
steps.solution: Route the second cohort through its own quota and edge cache while both regions share the origin shield. Inspect the separate edge hit/miss records and shared upstream transfers. These are explicit drawn routes, not a measured locality percentage or an automatic geo-router.
tradeoffs: Separate edge caches isolate admission but duplicate regional cache storage and cold fills. The shared shield can combine upstream misses for the same segment.
A cache hit ratio depends on this finite request sequence and cache policy. It does not establish a global traffic-locality target or production capacity.

steps.stage: Fall back from interrupted peer delivery
steps.interviewerPrompt: CDN egress costs are unsustainable during viral streams. Can viewers in the same region share segments directly without hurting buffering?
steps.solution: Enable the drawn peer path in each region and interrupt the first peer pool from four to seven seconds. Bounded peer attempts and circuit breaking allow segment requests to fall back to CDN delivery when peer transfer cannot succeed. Inspect playback completion, peer failures and CDN calls.
tradeoffs: Peer attempts can reduce CDN requests under the configured availability assumptions, while failed attempts add latency before fallback. Compare observed counts rather than assuming an offload percentage.
The simulation models peer transfer and deadline behavior without executing WebRTC, viewer upload scheduling or real device resource costs.

diagram.name: Global Video Streaming & CDN Architecture / Verify regional delivery
diagram.description: Three thousand viewers are split into two independently faultable regions. Playback requires a real manifest receipt; regional caches fetch through one shield and origin. Peer availability and admission are distinct from CDN delivery. Bytes are aggregate unicast, not measured video transport.

notes.text: Regional peers only assist cohorts in their own pool. Manifest metadata, regional cache copies and the shared shield are distinct state. Viewer CDN KiB plus peer KiB is end-user delivery; do not sum every network hop as unique delivered content. Crash either peer pool, either cache or the manifest independently. No codec, signaling, ICE or DRM is modeled.

social-feed.title: Scalable Social Media News Feed
social-feed.subtitle: System Design Interview: Fan-out on Read vs Write, Timeline Caching & Graph Traversal
social-feed.problemStatement: Design a social media news feed (like Twitter or Instagram) with instantaneous timeline loading, fan-out on write queues, and high-concurrency follower graph traversals.

steps.name: Fan-out on Read (Naive MVP)
steps.interviewerPrompt: Design a basic social feed where users publish posts and read recent posts from people they follow.
steps.solution: Users publish posts to an admitted Posts DB. Feed generation queries the database on the fly by looking up followees and sorting their recent posts.
tradeoffs: Read-time assembly scans bounded recent posts from followed users; work grows with candidate posts and the follow set.
Avoiding precomputed fanout reduces write amplification but shifts work onto each feed read. Compare observed work under the same bounded demand; this is not a production scaling estimate.

diagram.name: Scalable Social Media News Feed / Choose read-time assembly
diagram.description: Users and follower relations live in an independent social graph. Committed posts resolve their real audience before queueing fanout; feed reads join graph-selected posts with follower timelines. Bound admission, retries and delayed writes are separate executable components.

notes.text: Expand publication, graph, fanout and feed subsystems. Graph outages fail lookup, not fabricate empty audiences. Queue retries preserve post identity and timeline writes deduplicate recipient/post pairs. Early successful feed reads can still be stale. Change push/pull/hybrid on the post store to compare actual write amplification.

steps.name: Fan-out on Write with Asynchronous Queues
steps.stage: Fan-out on Write with Asynchronous Queues
steps.interviewerPrompt: How do we make feed loading instant (<20ms) for millions of readers?
steps.solution: Shift to Fan-out on Write: When a post is published, enqueue a background task. Fanout workers lookup followers and push the post ID into each follower's pre-computed in-memory Timeline.
tradeoffs: Precomputed timelines reduce read assembly work but introduce asynchronous freshness lag and recipient write amplification.
A large follow set produces more queued recipient writes per post; bounded fanout and timeline admission expose that pressure.
Recipient/post identity suppresses duplicate effects when a leased post retries.

steps.name: Separate committed work from a lost reply
steps.stage: Separate committed work from a lost reply
steps.interviewerPrompt: Which result is uncertain, and which state remains authoritative after reply delivery fails?
steps.solution: Drop replies briefly after work may have executed. A timeout establishes an uncertain acknowledgement, not proof that an effect did not occur. Inspect attempts and retained state; retries must preserve their operation identity.
tradeoffs: A smaller receive budget limits repeated work during an outage but moves transient failures to quarantine sooner. Dead-lettering does not itself repair a timeline.
Post acceptance acknowledges stored posts and queueing, not delivery to every follower. Compare missing-post observations with dead-letter records after recovery.
Timeline recipient/post identity prevents duplicate effects during retries. The synthetic graph and bounded retention do not establish production capacity.

steps.name: Bound retries and quarantine failed fanout
steps.stage: Bound retries and quarantine failed fanout
steps.interviewerPrompt: How do we handle billions of follow relationships with fast traversals, and what happens when timeline fanout workers crash?
steps.solution: Keep the existing separate graph authority and interrupt timeline writes until three seconds. Limit each queued post to two deliveries and route exhausted work to the dead-letter store. Later posts can complete after recovery; accepted posts whose fanout is quarantined remain absent from affected timelines until an operator explicitly repairs them.
